claim: In Diptera, the forewings power flight, whereas the hindwings have evolved into specialized structures called halteres.
source: In Diptera, the forewings power flight, whereas the hindwings have evolved into specialized structures called halteres, which provide rapid mechanosensory feedback for flight stabilization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Dipteran anatomy and is stated directly in the abstract.

claim: Halteres provide rapid mechanosensory feedback for flight stabilization.
source: In Diptera, the forewings power flight, whereas the hindwings have evolved into specialized structures called halteres, which provide rapid mechanosensory feedback for flight stabilization.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Wing and haltere motion is precisely phase-coordinated at high frequencies despite being actuated by independent muscles.
source: Although actuated by independent muscles, wing and haltere motion is precisely phase-coordinated at high frequencies.
evidence: This is a key observation supported by experimental data and previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Wingbeat frequency is a product of wing-thorax resonance.
source: Because wingbeat frequency is a product of wing-thorax resonance, any wear-and-tear of wings or thorax should impair flight ability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect flight mechanics.

claim: Wings and halteres are independently driven, coupled oscillators.
source: Here, we show that wings and halteres are independently driven, coupled oscillators.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data from wing clipping and haltere loading experiments.

claim: The wing-wing system is a strongly coupled oscillator.
source: The wing-wing system is a strongly coupled oscillator, whereas the wing-haltere system is weakly coupled through mechanical linkages that synchronize phase and frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that wings maintain identical frequencies even when one wing is clipped.

claim: The wing-haltere system is weakly coupled through mechanical linkages that synchronize phase and frequency.
source: The wing-wing system is a strongly coupled oscillator, whereas the wing-haltere system is weakly coupled through mechanical linkages that synchronize phase and frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that haltere frequency can decouple from wing frequency under certain conditions.

claim: The wing-haltere link acts in a unidirectional manner; altering wingbeat frequency affects haltere frequency, but not vice versa.
source: Wing-haltere link acts in a unidirectional manner; altering wingbeat frequency affects haltere frequency, but not vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from haltere loading experiments showing that changing haltere frequency does not affect wing frequency.

claim: Exoskeletal linkages ensure wing-haltere synchrony despite severe wing damage.
source: Exoskeletal linkages are thus key morphological features of the Dipteran thorax that ensure wing-haltere synchrony, despite severe wing damage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing maintained synchrony even with >50% wing length reduction.

claim: Flies are among the best exemplars of aerial agility.
source: Flies are among the best exemplars of aerial agility.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly flight capabilities.

claim: The Dipteran order encompasses a vast repertoire of flight types ranging from the exquisite hovering and maneuvering ability of hoverflies, to the stable trajectories of mosquitoes and rapid territorial chases in houseflies.
source: The Dipteran order encompasses a vast repertoire of flight types ranging from the exquisite hovering and maneuvering ability of hoverflies, to the stable trajectories of mosquitoes and rapid territorial chases in houseflies (Land and Collett, 1974).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Complex maneuvers require precise and rapid control, guided by sensory feedback from multiple modalities.
source: Such complex maneuvers require precise and rapid control, guided by sensory feedback from multiple modalities (Bender and Dickinson, 2006; Heide and Götz, 1996; Hengstenberg, 1993; Pringle, 1997; Sherman and Dickinson, 2003; Trimarchi and Schneiderman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Mechanosensory feedback from halteres is of particular importance for flight stability.
source: Of particular importance for flight stability is the mechanosensory feedback from halteres – the modified hindwings of flies – which sense gyroscopic forces during aerial maneuvers (Nalbach, 1994; Nalbach, 1993; Nalbach and Hengstenberg, 1994; Pringle, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Halteres sense gyroscopic forces during aerial maneuvers.
source: Of particular importance for flight stability is the mechanosensory feedback from halteres – the modified hindwings of flies – which sense gyroscopic forces during aerial maneuvers (Nalbach, 1994; Nalbach, 1993; Nalbach and Hengstenberg, 1994; Pringle, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: During flight, the halteres oscillate in a constant plane at frequencies that are identical to their flapping wings, and with a constant phase difference relative to the wings.
source: During flight, the halteres oscillate in a constant plane at frequencies that are identical to their flapping wings, and with a constant phase difference relative to the wings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about haltere function.

claim: During an aerial turn, an externally imposed change in the plane of haltere oscillation is resisted due to rotational inertia, causing Coriolis torques to act on the haltere base.
source: During an aerial turn, an externally imposed change in the plane of haltere oscillation is resisted due to rotational inertia, causing Coriolis torques to act on the haltere base.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the physics of haltere function.

claim: Mechanical strain in the haltere shaft due to Coriolis torques is sensed by multiple fields of campaniform sensillae distributed around its base.
source: Mechanical strain in the haltere shaft due to Coriolis torques is sensed by multiple fields of campaniform sensillae distributed around its base.
evidence: This is established knowledge about haltere anatomy and function.

claim: Campaniform sensillae encode the stroke-by-stroke status of aerial rotations and provide mechanosensory feedback to the wing muscles.
source: These encode the stroke-by-stroke status of aerial rotations and provide mechanosensory feedback to the wing muscles (Fayyazuddin and Dickinson, 1996; Yarger and Fox, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Haltere plays an additional role in mediating visually driven maneuvers.
source: In addition to detecting body rotations, haltere plays an additional role in mediating visually driven maneuvers; visual feedback drives haltere-steering muscles and alters the haltere mechanosensory feedback (Chan and Dickinson, 1996; Dickerson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Visual feedback drives haltere-steering muscles and alters the haltere mechanosensory feedback.
source: In addition to detecting body rotations, haltere plays an additional role in mediating visually driven maneuvers; visual feedback drives haltere-steering muscles and alters the haltere mechanosensory feedback (Chan and Dickinson, 1996; Dickerson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The relative phase difference between the feedback from wing and haltere mechanosensors determines the activity patterns in wing-steering muscles.
source: Importantly, the relative phase difference between the feedback from wing and haltere mechanosensors determines the activity patterns in wing-steering muscles (Fayyazuddin and Dickinson, 1999; Fox et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: During flight, the two wings of flies move exactly in-phase relative to each other.
source: During flight, the two wings of flies move exactly in-phase relative to each other, whereas halteres move at a constant phase offset relative to wings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly wing kinematics.

claim: Halteres move at a constant phase offset relative to wings.
source: During flight, the two wings of flies move exactly in-phase relative to each other, whereas halteres move at a constant phase offset relative to wings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fly wing-haltere kinematics.

claim: This precise phase coordination is maintained at wingbeat frequencies that far exceed 100 Hz.
source: This precise phase coordination is maintained at wingbeat frequencies that far exceed 100 Hz (Deora et al., 2015; Hall et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Even slight asymmetries in the bilateral wing motions can result in significantly large torques on the body during flight.
source: Because even slight asymmetries in the bilateral wing motions can result in significantly large torques on the body during flight (Fry et al., 2003), the phase and frequency synchronization of the wing-haltere kinematics is a core feature of Dipteran flight, any deviation from which may signal either a self-generated aerial turn or an unwanted perturbation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The phase and frequency synchronization of the wing-haltere kinematics is a core feature of Dipteran flight.
source: Because even slight asymmetries in the bilateral wing motions can result in significantly large torques on the body during flight (Fry et al., 2003), the phase and frequency synchronization of the wing-haltere kinematics is a core feature of Dipteran flight, any deviation from which may signal either a self-generated aerial turn or an unwanted perturbation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work and general principles of flight control.

claim: The wing-haltere system acts as a complex resonant box.
source: The wing-haltere system acts as a complex resonant box.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect flight mechanics.

claim: In flies, wings are actuated by two sets of antagonistic indirect flight muscles aligned dorso-longitudinally and dorso-ventrally within the thorax.
source: In flies, wings are actuated by two sets of antagonistic indirect flight muscles aligned dorso-longitudinally and dorso-ventrally within the thorax (Deora et al., 2017; Dickinson and Tu, 1997; Pringle, 1949).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Indirect flight muscles do not directly articulate at the wing base, but instead attach to the thorax, thereby indirectly powering the wing motions.
source: These muscles do not directly articulate at the wing base, but instead attach to the thorax, thereby indirectly powering the wing motions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about indirect flight muscle anatomy.

claim: The activation of indirect flight muscles is myogenic; contraction in one set of muscles triggers delayed contraction of the other and vice versa, setting up resonant cycles of oscillations of the entire thorax.
source: Their activation is myogenic; hence, contraction in one set of muscles triggers delayed contraction of the other and vice versa, setting up resonant cycles of oscillations of the entire thorax (e.g., Deora et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A complex wing hinge transforms oscillatory deformations of the thorax into large-amplitude wing strokes.
source: A complex wing hinge transforms oscillatory deformations of the thorax into large-amplitude wing strokes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect wing mechanics.

claim: The indirect flight muscles require neural stimulation to remain in an active state, but the frequency of stimulation is typically an order of magnitude lower than resonant thoracic oscillations.
source: The indirect flight muscles require neural stimulation to remain in an active state, but the frequency of stimulation is typically an order of magnitude lower than resonant thoracic oscillations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asynchronous muscle function.

claim: The attitude of the wing is finely adjusted on a stroke-to-stroke basis by a set of steering muscles that are under direct neuronal control.
source: The attitude of the wing is finely adjusted on a stroke-to-stroke basis by a set of steering muscles that are under direct neuronal control (Lindsay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The frequency characteristics of Dipteran wing movements are set by the resonance frequency, which in turn is determined primarily by the wing-thoracic morphology.
source: Thus, the frequency characteristics of Dipteran wing movements are set by the resonance frequency, which in turn is determined primarily by the wing-thoracic morphology.
evidence: This is an inference based on established principles of resonant systems.

claim: Any alteration in the wing length causes corresponding changes in their inertial and aerodynamic loads, and hence in the frequency of the wingbeat.
source: Thus, any alteration in the wing length causes corresponding changes in their inertial and aerodynamic loads, and hence in the frequency of the wingbeat.
evidence: This is an inference based on established principles of resonant systems.

claim: The motion of each haltere is powered by a single asynchronous muscle whose contractions activate its upstroke, whereas the downstroke is thought to be entirely passive.
source: Unlike wings, the motion of each haltere is powered by a single asynchronous muscle whose contractions activate its upstroke, whereas the downstroke is thought to be entirely passive (Chan et al., 1998; Pringle, 1949).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The precise coordination of wings and halteres is mediated by mechanical linkages within the thorax that ensure tight coupling of phase and frequency.
source: Although wingbeat frequency depends on the wing-thorax morphology, the precise coordination of wings and halteres is mediated by mechanical linkages within the thorax that ensure tight coupling of phase and frequency (Figure 1B, Deora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The scutellar link is embedded within the scutellum and ensures that both wings are synchronized.
source: One linkage, the scutellar link (alternatively, wing-wing link, in orange in Figure 1B), is embedded within the scutellum and ensures that both wings are synchronized.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge ensures precise coordination of wings and halteres.
source: A second linkage, the sub-epimeral ridge (alternatively, wing-haltere link, highlighted by green arrows in Figure 1B), ensures precise coordination of wings and halteres.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge linkage ensures only weak coupling of the wing-haltere synchrony, but breaks down when wingbeat frequency exceeds a threshold value.
source: This linkage ensures only weak coupling of the wing-haltere synchrony, but breaks down when wingbeat frequency exceeds a threshold value (Deora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wings of insects often undergo significant natural wear-and-tear during the lifetime of an adult insect.
source: However, wings of insects often undergo significant natural wear-and-tear during the lifetime of an adult insect (Hayes and Wall, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Wing damage alters both frequency and aerodynamic force generation of the flapping wings.
source: Wing damage alters both frequency and aerodynamic force generation of the flapping wings (Hedenström et al., 2001; Kihlström et al., 2021; Muijres et al., 2017), thus posing a challenge to the overall coordination of wing motion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Wing damage is typically asymmetric and can affect maneuverability.
source: Such damage is typically asymmetric and can affect maneuverability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of wing damage in the wild.

claim: In insects such as bumblebees and dragonflies, wing damage leads to decreased success in hunting and also greater mortality.
source: Not surprisingly, in insects such as bumblebees and dragonflies, wing damage leads to decreased success in hunting and also greater mortality (Cartar, 1992; Combes et al., 2010; Haas and Cartar, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Even after drastic reduction in the length of one wing by >50% of the original length, the frequencies of the clipped and intact wings were always identical and did not drastically reduce from their intact values.
source: Even after drastic reduction in the length of one wing by >50% of the original length, the frequencies of the clipped and intact wings were always identical and did not drastically reduce from their intact values (Figure 2A; for additional data, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1, p=0.623; number of flies, n = 6, one-sided, Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the maximum wing difference).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and statistical analysis.

claim: The overall wingbeat frequency is determined by the frequency of the intact wing.
source: Thus, the overall wingbeat frequency is determined by the frequency of the intact wing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that clipping one wing does not significantly alter frequency.

claim: Lesioning the scutellum disrupts the synchrony of the two wings and causes them to flap at different frequencies if the length of one is altered.
source: Fourier analysis of the time series of wing motion shows that both wings oscillated at very different frequencies. Thus, unlike the intact scutellum case in which frequency synchronization was robust despite wing damage (Figure 2A), the wings of a scutellum-lesioned fly were decoupled from each other (Figure 2B, additional data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, p=0.022; n = 5, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the maximum wing difference).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and statistical analysis.

claim: Lesioning the scutellum disrupts and reattaching completely restores the phase coordination between both wings.
source: Our previous work shows that lesioning the scutellum disrupts and reattaching completely restores the phase coordination between both wings (Deora et al., 2015); thus, scutellar integrity is essential to ensure precise coupling of both phase and frequency of the two wings, and imparts robust synchronization even if one or both wings are slightly damaged or torn.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Scutellar integrity is essential to ensure precise coupling of both phase and frequency of the two wings.
source: Our previous work shows that lesioning the scutellum disrupts and reattaching completely restores the phase coordination between both wings (Deora et al., 2015); thus, scutellar integrity is essential to ensure precise coupling of both phase and frequency of the two wings, and imparts robust synchronization even if one or both wings are slightly damaged or torn.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and previous work.

claim: The two wings are strongly coupled by the scutellar link.
source: Together, these data show that the two wings are strongly coupled by the scutellar link.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that wings remain synchronized when the scutellum is intact.

claim: Freely flying insects typically offset the effects of wing damage by altering their wing kinematics, particularly their wing amplitude.
source: Wing damage not only alters the resonant frequency of the wing-thorax system but also reduces the aerodynamic force generation by the wings. Freely flying insects typically offset the effects of wing damage by altering their wing kinematics, particularly their wing amplitude (Fernández et al., 2012; Kihlström et al., 2021; Muijres et al., 2017; Vance and Roberts, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In tethered flies with an intact thorax, the amplitude of clipped wing reduced as the wing was shortened, but there was no significant change in intact wing's amplitude.
source: In tethered flies with an intact thorax, the amplitude of clipped wing reduced as the wing was shorterened, but there was no significant change in intact wing's amplitude(p=2.1e-4 for clipped, 0.218 for intact wings, Kruskal–Wallis H-test, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and statistical analysis.

claim: Neither the clipped nor the intact wings of tethered flies with a lesioned scutellum showed a significant difference in wing amplitude with reduction in wing length.
source: In contrast, neither the clipped nor the intact wings of tethered flies with a lesioned scutellum showed a significant difference in wing amplitude with reduction in wing length (p=0.067 and 0.184 for clipped and intact wings, respectively, Kruskal–Wallis H-test, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and statistical analysis.

claim: Slight symmetrical clipping of both wings resulted in a small increase in wingbeat frequency and concomitant increase in haltere frequency.
source: Slight symmetrical clipping of both wings resulted in a small increase in wingbeat frequency and concomitant increase in haltere frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work.

claim: With further symmetrical reduction of wing length, wingbeat frequencies exceeded ~150% of the initial values, but the halteres failed to keep pace with the wings.
source: However, with further symmetrical reduction of wing length, wingbeat frequencies exceeded ~150% of the initial values, but the halteres failed to keep pace with the wings.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from previous work.

claim: When wingbeat frequencies exceed ~150% of initial values, haltere frequency drops closer to their natural frequency, suggesting that their coupling is weak.
source: In such conditions, haltere frequency dropped closer to their natural frequency, suggesting that their coupling was weak (Figure 3, control haltere [in blue]; Deora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and previous work.

claim: The control (right) haltere frequency matched the wing frequency more robustly than the lesioned left haltere-wing pair.
source: Our data were consistent with this hypothesis; the control (right) haltere frequency matched the wing frequency more robustly than the lesioned left haltere-wing pair (Figure 3A, p=0.039 for wing-treatment haltere pair and p=0.657 for wing-control haltere pair, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test at wing length bin = [0.6, 0.7], n = 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and statistical analysis.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge weakly couples wing and haltere oscillation.
source: Together, these results suggest that the sub-epimeral ridge weakly couples wing and haltere oscillation.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that haltere frequency can decouple from wing frequency when the sub-epimeral ridge is lesioned.

claim: Haltere motion can accommodate small to moderate changes in wingbeat frequency but fails if these changes are large.
source: Haltere motion can accommodate small to moderate changes in wingbeat frequency but fails if these changes are large.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that haltere frequency decouples from wing frequency at high frequencies.

claim: In flies with unilaterally lesioned sub-epimeral ridge, the overall changes in wingbeat frequency were relatively moderate (~60 Hz) even after shortening the wing to the smallest wing length.
source: In flies with unilaterally lesioned sub-epimeral ridge, the overall changes in wingbeat frequency (frequency of intact wing compared to the frequency at the shortest wing length) were relatively moderate (~60 Hz) even after shortening the wing to the smallest wing length (Figure 4, data for intact flies from Deora et al., 2015, p<0.05, Kruskal–Wallis ANOVA followed by the post hoc Tukey–Kramer multi-comparison test, n; eight intact flies, six flies for the other three treatments).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and statistical analysis.

claim: In flies with both sub-epimeral ridges lesioned, the increase in wingbeat frequency was even further restricted (<40 Hz).
source: In these flies, the increase in wingbeat frequency was even further restricted (<40 Hz).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Clipping wings of the haltere-ablated flies resulted in significantly elevated wingbeat frequency (by ~90 Hz) as compared with flies with both sub-epimeral ridges lesioned.
source: Clipping wings of the haltere-ablated flies resulted in significantly elevated wingbeat frequency (by ~90 Hz, Figure 4) as compared with flies with both sub-epimeral ridges lesioned (p<0.05) but similar to flies with an intact sub-epimeral ridge.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and statistical analysis.

claim: Mechanical integrity of the thoracic linkages most likely determines wingbeat frequency.
source: This suggests that mechanical integrity of these linkages most likely determines wingbeat frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data comparing lesioned and ablated conditions.

claim: The mechanical integrity of the entire thoracic linkage system, including both the scutellum and sub-epimeral ridge, is essential to maintain the resonant properties of the thorax.
source: Hence, the mechanical integrity of the entire thoracic linkage system, including both the scutellum and sub-epimeral ridge, is essential to maintain the resonant properties of the thorax.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that lesioning linkages reduces frequency changes.

claim: Small loads did not affect haltere frequency, but as the load increased beyond a threshold, haltere frequency decreased in discrete steps.
source: Small loads did not affect haltere frequency, but as the load increased beyond a threshold, haltere frequency decreased in discrete steps.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from haltere loading experiments.

claim: Wingbeat frequency remained constant when halteres were loaded.
source: However, wingbeat frequency remained constant in these experiments (Figure 5; for individual fly data, see Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F, p=0.014; one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test for left loaded haltere and wing pair at load2 and load3, n = 6 flies).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of sub-epimeral ridge is unidirectional, which couples haltere motion to wing motion but not vice versa.
source: Thus, the effect of sub-epimeral ridge is a unidirectional, which couples haltere motion to wing motion but not vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that loading halteres does not affect wing frequency.

claim: Haltere frequency recovered and again matched wingbeat frequency after the load was removed.
source: To rule out the possibility that loading the haltere irreversibly damaged haltere muscles or the sub-epimeral ridge, we detached the load and confirmed that haltere frequency recovered and again matched wingbeat frequency (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and supplementary figures.

claim: Mechanical linkages enable robust frequency-phase output despite asymmetric wing damage.
source: Mechanical linkages enable robust frequency-phase output despite asymmetric wing damage
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Physical damage to the wings of adult insects is irreversible and potentially deleterious for their fitness.
source: Physical damage to the wings of adult insects is irreversible and potentially deleterious for their fitness.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect wing damage.

claim: Wings of certain insects have flexible costal break or specific venation patterns that prevent wing damage.
source: Wings of certain insects have flexible costal break or specific venation patterns that prevent wing damage (Mountcastle and Combes, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Insects incur wing damage in the wild due to factors such as predation and age.
source: However, despite such adaptations, insects incur wing damage in the wild due to factors such as predation and age (Cartar, 1992; Hayes and Wall, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When one or both wings are damaged, the overall aerodynamic load reduces, thereby increasing the frequency of thoracic and wing oscillations.
source: When one or both wings are damaged, the overall aerodynamic load reduces, thereby increasing the frequency of thoracic and wing oscillations (Deora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The linkages may be viewed as evolutionary adaptations that impart robustness to wing motion in case of damage or wear-and-tear.
source: The linkages described here ensure that the phase and frequency matching between wings and halteres is robust despite significant changes in wingbeat frequency, and hence they may be viewed as evolutionary adaptations that impart robustness to wing motion in case of damage or wear-and-tear.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional significance of the linkages.

claim: Natural wing damage is typically asymmetric.
source: Natural wing damage is typically asymmetric.
evidence: This is established knowledge about wing damage in nature.

claim: Shortening only one wing by as much as 50% did not significantly alter the resonant frequency of thorax.
source: Although shortening both wings symmetrically results in elevated wingbeat frequencies (Deora et al., 2015), shortening only one wing by as much as 50% did not significantly alter the resonant frequency of thorax.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The resonant frequency is dictated primarily by the wing with greater aerodynamic load.
source: This suggests that the resonant frequency is dictated primarily by the wing with greater aerodynamic load.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that asymmetric clipping does not significantly alter frequency.

claim: In flies with an intact scutellar linkage, asymmetric changes in wing length did not alter the overall synchrony; wings remained bilaterally coordinated, regardless of their length.
source: Importantly, in flies with an intact scutellar linkage, asymmetric changes in wing length did not alter the overall synchrony; wings remained bilaterally coordinated, regardless of their length (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Freely flying flies and bees with damaged wings increase their wingbeat frequency to compensate for the reduced lift.
source: Freely flying flies and bees with damaged wings increase their wingbeat frequency to compensate for the reduced lift (Hedenström et al., 2001; Muijres et al., 2017; Vance and Roberts, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Flies and bees with asymmetric wing damage balance the roll torque by flapping the damaged wing at greater amplitudes.
source: Moreover, flies and bees with asymmetric wing damage balance the roll torque by flapping the damaged wing at greater amplitudes (Muijres et al., 2017; Vance and Roberts, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In tethered flies with intact thorax, asymmetric wing damage did not increase wingbeat frequency.
source: In our experiments with tethered flies, however, asymmetric wing damage in flies with intact thorax did not increase wingbeat frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: In tethered flies with intact thorax, the clipped wing flapped at reduced wing amplitudes.
source: Instead, in these flies, the clipped wing flapped at reduced wing amplitudes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The increase in wingbeat frequency and the amplitude modulation that is observed in freely flying insects with damaged wings may be an active response that enables compensation for the loss of the lift due to wing damage.
source: These results suggest that the increase in wingbeat frequency and the amplitude modulation that is observed in freely flying insects with damaged wings may be an active response that enables compensation for the loss of the lift due to wing damage.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison of tethered and free-flying behavior.

claim: Lesioning the scutellum completely decoupled the frequencies of the two wings of different lengths; shortened wings oscillated at frequencies up to twice that of the intact wing and cause irregular wing motion.
source: Lesioning the scutellum completely decoupled the frequencies of the two wings of different lengths; shortened wings oscillated at frequencies up to twice that of the intact wing and cause irregular wing motion.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The indirect flight muscles on the two sides are, in principle, capable of operating at different frequencies, but are constrained to flap synchronously by the scutellar link.
source: In the experiments in which the scutellar link was lesioned, the shortened wing flapped at higher frequency than the intact wing. This shows that the indirect flight muscles on the two sides are, in principle, capable of operating at different frequencies, but are constrained to flap synchronously by the scutellar link.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that wings can flap at different frequencies when the scutellum is lesioned.

claim: Indirect flight muscles aid the direct flight muscles in power modulation and kinematic control of wings.
source: These results are consistent with the idea that indirect flight muscles aid the direct flight muscles in power modulation and kinematic control of wings (Gordon and Dickinson, 2006; Lehmann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In intact flies, power modulation occurs under constraints of equal bilateral wingbeat frequency and phase, which leaves open the possibility that amplitude or stroke plane can be modulated by power muscles.
source: In intact flies, power modulation occurs under constraints of equal bilateral wingbeat frequency and phase, which leaves open the possibility that amplitude or stroke plane can be modulated by power muscles.
evidence: This is speculation based on the constraints imposed by the scutellar link.

claim: During turns, the two sets of dorsolongitudinal muscles can be differentially activated by their motor neurons, potentially leading to differential power output.
source: For instance, during turns, the two sets of dorsolongitudinal muscles can be differentially activated by their motor neurons (Gordon and Dickinson, 2006; Lehmann et al., 2013; Sponberg and Daniel, 2012), potentially leading to differential power output.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Asymmetric wing damage in hawkmoths results in net torque on the body.
source: Moreover, asymmetric wing damage results in net torque on the body in hawkmoths (Fernández et al., 2012; also see, Kihlström et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Asymmetric wing damage in hawkmoths causes activation delay in the dorsoventral power muscle, resulting in a voluntary yaw-like maneuver towards the undamaged side.
source: Asymmetric wing damage in hawkmoths causes activation delay in the dorsoventral power muscle, resulting in a voluntary yaw-like maneuver towards the undamaged side, perhaps to compensate for the reduced lift on the damaged side.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The indirect, asynchronous flight muscles of flies could also modulate power output of the ipsilateral wing, independent of the contralateral power muscles.
source: Our results suggest that, like hawkmoths, the indirect, asynchronous flight muscles of flies could also modulate power output of the ipsilateral wing, independent of the contralateral power muscles.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with hawkmoths and the experimental results.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge synchronizes the frequency and phase difference between wings and halteres on each side.
source: The sub-epimeral ridge synchronizes the frequency and phase difference between wings and halteres on each side (Figure 3, Deora et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The precise phase difference between wings and halteres is likely the outcome of the variation in the thoracic and linkage anatomy across Diptera and the physics of coupled, driven oscillator systems.
source: It is not clear how the precise phase difference is set in these flies, but these parameters are likely the outcome of the variation in the thoracic and linkage anatomy across Diptera and the physics of coupled, driven oscillator systems.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanisms determining phase relationships.

claim: When wing and haltere frequencies are decoupled by loading the haltere, the haltere oscillates at an altered phase relative to the wing, even when sub-epimeral ridge is intact.
source: Indeed, when wing and haltere frequencies are decoupled by loading the haltere (Figure 5), the haltere oscillates at an altered phase relative to the wing, even when sub-epimeral ridge is intact (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Wing frequency is thought to be determined primarily by the stretch-activation properties of the indirect flight muscles.
source: Their frequency, on the other hand, is thought to be determined primarily by the stretch-activation properties of their main driving muscles – the indirect flight muscles for wings, and haltere muscles (or Pringle's muscle) for halteres.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asynchronous muscle function.

claim: Haltere frequency is thought to be determined primarily by the stretch-activation properties of the haltere muscles.
source: Their frequency, on the other hand, is thought to be determined primarily by the stretch-activation properties of their main driving muscles – the indirect flight muscles for wings, and haltere muscles (or Pringle's muscle) for halteres.
evidence: This is established knowledge about asynchronous muscle function.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge couples haltere frequency to wingbeat frequency, and their vibration frequency is fine-tuned by this linkage and the overall thoracic geometry.
source: Because the sub-epimeral ridge couples haltere frequency to wingbeat frequency, their vibration frequency is fine-tuned by this linkage and the overall thoracic geometry.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing coupling between wing and haltere frequencies.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge weakly couples wings and halteres, with its stiffness limited by its material strength and geometry.
source: The sub-epimeral ridge weakly couples wings and halteres. Its stiffness is limited by its material strength and geometry, and it can ensure coordination of wing-haltere frequency close to original frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and principles of mechanical coupling.

claim: At wingbeat frequencies greater than about 150% of the original frequency, the haltere frequency reverts to a value that is closer to or equal to its natural frequency.
source: At wingbeat frequencies greater than about 150% of the original frequency, the haltere frequency reverts to a value that is closer to or equal to its natural frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: The behavior of the sub-epimeral ridge is typical of independently driven oscillators, coupled by a mechanical element of finite coupling strength.
source: This behavior is typical of independently driven oscillators, coupled by a mechanical element of finite coupling strength (Strogatz, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to work on coupled oscillators.

claim: The sub-epimeral ridge acts in a unidirectional manner; moderate changes in wingbeat frequency alter the haltere frequency, but not vice versa.
source: Moreover, the sub-epimeral ridge acts in a unidirectional manner (Figure 5); moderate changes in wingbeat frequency alter the haltere frequency, but not vice versa.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The unidirectional nature of the sub-epimeral ridge may be the outcome of the large difference between the wing and haltere loads (and therefore inertia), and their respective muscles.
source: This may be the outcome of the large difference between the wing and haltere loads (and therefore inertia), and their respective muscles.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism underlying unidirectional coupling.

claim: The aerodynamic load on the wings determines flapping frequency, and the halteres merely follow the wings.
source: Our experiments show that the aerodynamic load on the wings determines flapping frequency, and the halteres merely follow the wings.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that wing frequency is not affected by haltere loading.

claim: Aberrant haltere feedback due to a lesioned sub-epimeral ridge causes a reduction in the amplitude of the ipsilateral wings as compared to the contralateral (intact) side.
source: Aberrant haltere feedback due to a lesioned sub-epimeral ridge causes a reduction in the amplitude of the ipsilateral wings as compared to the contralateral (intact) side.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: All insects that possess asynchronous flight muscles must rely on linkages for wing-wing coordination.
source: Although our study was focused on Dipteran insects, several implications of this study extend beyond Diptera. Indeed, all insects that possess asynchronous flight muscles must rely on linkages for wing-wing coordination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the principles of asynchronous muscle function and the findings of the study.

claim: Insects with asynchronous flight muscles include insects of the orders Hymenoptera (e.g., wasps, honeybees, etc.) and Coleoptera (e.g., beetles), which are hyper-diverse.
source: These include insects of the orders Hymenoptera (e.g., wasps, honeybees, etc.) and Coleoptera (e.g., beetles), which are hyper-diverse.
evidence: This is established knowledge about insect taxonomy and muscle types.

claim: In insects with asynchronous flight muscles, the bilateral coordination of wings is unlikely to be achieved through direct neural control as they flap at very high wingbeat frequencies.
source: In these insects, as in Diptera (which are also hyper-diverse), the bilateral coordination of wings is unlikely to be achieved through direct neural control as they flap at very high wingbeat frequencies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of neural control at high frequencies.

claim: Similar linkages to those found in Diptera likely exist in Hymenoptera and Coleoptera.
source: We therefore predict that similar linkages also exist in these insect taxa.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional requirements of insects with asynchronous flight muscles.

claim: In insects with asynchronous flight muscles, it is likely that relative coordination between the front and the hindwings is mediated by passive linkages analogous to the sub-epimeral ridge in Diptera.
source: In such insects, it is also likely that relative coordination between the front and the hindwings is mediated by passive linkages analogous to the sub-epimeral ridge in Diptera.
evidence: This is speculation based on the functional requirements of insects with asynchronous flight muscles.

claim: Thoracic linkages may play a very important role in miniature insects, in which there are fewer muscle groups for higher-level control.
source: Thoracic linkages may also play a very important role in miniature insects, in which there are fewer muscle groups for higher-level control.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of linkages in miniature insects.

claim: Extreme miniaturization in insects of the order Diptera, Hymenoptera, and Coleoptera poses severe physiological and biomechanical constraints on the organism.
source: Extreme miniaturization in insects of the order Diptera, Hymenoptera, and Coleoptera (Polilov, 2015) poses severe physiological and biomechanical constraints on the organism (Polilov, 2012; Sane, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Smaller wings generate reduced aerodynamic lift, so miniature insects must flap at increased frequencies to generate enough lift to stay aloft.
source: Because smaller wings generate reduced aerodynamic lift, miniature insects must flap at increased frequencies to generate enough lift to stay aloft.
evidence: This is an inference based on principles of aerodynamics and scaling.

claim: In miniature insects, thoracic linkages are likely to play a key role in mediating synchronization of the wings, while also constraining their degrees of freedom.
source: In such insects, thoracic linkages are likely to play a key role in mediating synchronization of the wings, while also constraining their degrees of freedom.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of linkages in miniature insects.

claim: Small body sizes are associated with rapid wingbeat frequencies, often at rates much greater than possible through direct neural control.
source: Small body sizes are also associated with rapid wingbeat frequencies, often at rates much greater than possible through direct neural control (Dudley, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The thoracic morphology of the fly plays an important role in providing robust wing coordination despite wing damage.
source: The key results in this paper show that the thoracic morphology of the fly plays an important role in providing robust wing coordination despite wing damage.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Wild-caught black soldier flies, H. illucens, were used in the experiments.
source: Wild-caught black soldier flies, H. illucens, were enclosed in vials filled with a medium of corn flour and agar mixed with yeast powder.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Three high-speed cameras were used to film the insects in flight at a resolution of 800 × 600 pixels at 2000 frames per second.
source: We used three high-speed cameras (v7.3 Phantom camera, Vision Research Inc, Wayne, NJ) to film the insects in flight at a resolution of 800 × 600 pixels at 2000 frames per second (~15–20 times the wingbeat frequency) and 100 μs exposure.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Three cameras (one top view and two side views) captured the 3D motion of both pairs of wings and halteres.
source: Three cameras (one top view and two side views) captured the 3D motion of both pairs of wings and halteres (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods shown in Figure 1A.
